name: Angle sums (lines, triangle, polygon)
statement: \text{angles on a line}=180^\circ;\ \triangle: A+B+C=180^\circ;\ n\text{-gon}: (n-2)180^\circ
conditions: n \ge 3 \text{ (a polygon has at least 3 sides)}
derivation: A straight line is a half-turn, so angles on one side of it at a point add to $180^\circ$.
Through the apex $P$ draw a line parallel to $QR$.
Alternate angles: the two outer angles at $P$ equal $\angle Q$ and $\angle R$.
Those two plus $\angle P$ lie on the straight line: $P+Q+R=180^\circ$.
Diagonals from one vertex cut an $n$-gon into $n-2$ triangles, so the angle sum is $(n-2)\times180^\circ$.
visual_proof: A line through the apex parallel to the base copies the two base angles beside the apex angle (alternate angles), and the three together make a straight line.
shortcut: Each interior angle of a regular $n$-gon $=\frac{(n-2)180^\circ}{n}$; each exterior angle $=\frac{360^\circ}{n}$.
common_traps: Taking R = Q + 26 instead of Q - 26 gives 3Q = 134 and a non-option.
Stopping at Q = 62° and not finding P.
Using n × 180° for a polygon instead of (n - 2) × 180° (overshoots by 360°).

diagram.alt_text: Triangle PQR with angle Q 62°, R 36°, P 82°. A line XY through P parallel to QR shows 62° and 36° beside the 82° at P, together a straight angle.

import math, random
import sympy as sp
random.seed(0)

def angle(at, p, q):
    v1 = (p[0] - at[0], p[1] - at[1]); v2 = (q[0] - at[0], q[1] - at[1])
    c = (v1[0] * v2[0] + v1[1] * v2[1]) / (math.hypot(*v1) * math.hypot(*v2))
    return math.degrees(math.acos(max(-1.0, min(1.0, c))))

# triangle: A + B + C = 180 on random triangles
for _ in range(2000):
    A, B, C = [(random.uniform(-10, 10), random.uniform(-10, 10)) for _ in range(3)]
    area2 = abs((B[0]-A[0])*(C[1]-A[1]) - (C[0]-A[0])*(B[1]-A[1]))
    if area2 < 1e-3:
        continue
    assert math.isclose(angle(A, B, C) + angle(B, A, C) + angle(C, A, B), 180, abs_tol=1e-7)

# angles on a line: a ray from a point on a line splits 180
for _ in range(500):
    t = random.uniform(0.01, math.pi - 0.01)
    O, L, R, P = (0, 0), (-1, 0), (1, 0), (math.cos(t), math.sin(t))
    assert math.isclose(angle(O, L, P) + angle(O, P, R), 180, abs_tol=1e-7)

# convex n-gon: interior angle sum = (n-2)*180
for _ in range(500):
    n = random.randint(3, 12)
    ts = sorted(random.uniform(0, 2 * math.pi) for _ in range(n))
    if min((ts[(i + 1) % n] - ts[i]) % (2 * math.pi) for i in range(n)) < 1e-3:
        continue
    pts = [(math.cos(t), math.sin(t)) for t in ts]
    s = sum(angle(pts[i], pts[i - 1], pts[(i + 1) % n]) for i in range(n))
    assert math.isclose(s, (n - 2) * 180, abs_tol=1e-6)

# worked example: P - Q = 20, Q - R = 26
P, Q, R = sp.symbols("P Q R")
sol = sp.solve([P + Q + R - 180, P - Q - 20, Q - R - 26], [P, Q, R])
assert sol == {P: 82, Q: 62, R: 36}
assert [82, 46, 52, 92].index(sol[P]) == 0          # option A

# boundary n = 3: the polygon formula gives the triangle sum; n = 2 gives 0 (no polygon)
f = lambda n: (n - 2) * 180
assert f(3) == 180 and f(4) == 360 and f(2) == 0
print("BOUNDARY_OK")

name: Exterior angle theorem
statement: \text{exterior angle}=\text{sum of the two interior opposite angles}
derivation: Produce $BC$ to $D$; $\angle ACD$ is the exterior angle at $C$.
On the line: $\angle ACD = 180^\circ - \angle ACB$.
Angle sum: $\angle A + \angle B = 180^\circ - \angle ACB$ ([[f:geometry.triangle-angle-sum]]).
Same right-hand side, so $\angle ACD = \angle A + \angle B$.
visual_proof: A line through C parallel to BA splits the exterior angle into a copy of angle A (alternate angles) and a copy of angle B (corresponding angles).
common_traps: Adding the adjacent interior angle (angle C) instead of the two opposite ones.
Setting the equal angles opposite the wrong sides: AC = BC makes angles A and B equal, not A and C.
Answering ∠ACD = 140° when the question asks for a difference.

diagram.alt_text: Triangle ABC with AC = BC, BC produced to D. Angles A and B are 70° each and the exterior angle ACD is 140°.

random.seed(0)

def angle(at, p, q):
    v1 = (p[0] - at[0], p[1] - at[1]); v2 = (q[0] - at[0], q[1] - at[1])
    c = (v1[0] * v2[0] + v1[1] * v2[1]) / (math.hypot(*v1) * math.hypot(*v2))
    return math.degrees(math.acos(max(-1.0, min(1.0, c))))

for _ in range(2000):
    A, B, C = [(random.uniform(-10, 10), random.uniform(-10, 10)) for _ in range(3)]
    if abs((B[0]-A[0])*(C[1]-A[1]) - (C[0]-A[0])*(B[1]-A[1])) < 1e-3:
        continue
    s = random.uniform(0.1, 3)
    D = (C[0] + s * (C[0] - B[0]), C[1] + s * (C[1] - B[1]))     # BC produced to D
    assert math.isclose(angle(C, A, D), angle(A, B, C) + angle(B, A, C), abs_tol=1e-7)

# worked example: AC = BC, angle BAC = 70
B_ = 70                     # angle ABC = angle BAC (opposite equal sides)
ACD = 70 + B_               # exterior angle at C
assert ACD - B_ == 70       # option B
# check on coordinates: C at origin, CB and CA length 5, angle ACB = 40

assert math.isclose(angle(Bp, A, C), 70, abs_tol=1e-9) and math.isclose(angle(C, A, D), 140, abs_tol=1e-9)

name: Isosceles triangle properties
statement: AB=AC \Rightarrow \angle B=\angle C;\ \text{altitude from } A \text{ bisects } BC \text{ and } \angle A
derivation: Drop $AD \perp BC$.
$\triangle ABD$ and $\triangle ACD$: hypotenuses $AB=AC$, leg $AD$ common, so congruent by RHS ([[f:geometry.congruence-criteria]]).
Corresponding parts: $\angle B=\angle C$, $BD=DC$, $\angle BAD=\angle CAD$.
Converse: $\angle B=\angle C \Rightarrow AB=AC$ (equal angles face equal sides).
visual_proof: Fold the triangle along the altitude from the apex: the two halves match exactly, so the base angles coincide and the foot is the midpoint of the base.
shortcut: Apex angle $=180^\circ-2\times$base angle; base angle $=\frac{180^\circ-\text{apex}}{2}$.
common_traps: Taking 80° as the apex angle and halving: (180 - 80)/2 = 50° (option C).
Equal angles sit opposite the equal sides; with XY = XZ they are at Y and Z, not at X.
Two radii of a circle make an isosceles triangle; missing this stalls circle questions.

diagram.alt_text: Isosceles triangle XYZ with XY = XZ, base angles Y and Z of 80°, apex angle X of 20°, and the altitude XM meeting YZ at its midpoint M at a right angle.

name: Equilateral triangle properties
statement: h=\frac{\sqrt3}2a;\ R=\frac a{\sqrt3},\ r=\frac a{2\sqrt3};\ \text{a chord equal to the radius subtends } 60^\circ
derivation: All sides $a$, all angles $60^\circ$; the altitude bisects the base.
Half-triangle: $h^2=a^2-\left(\frac a2\right)^2=\frac{3a^2}{4}$, so $h=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}a$.
Centroid, circumcentre and incentre coincide and split $h$ as $2:1$ ([[f:geometry.median-apollonius]]).
$R=\frac23h=\frac{a}{\sqrt3}$, $r=\frac13h=\frac{a}{2\sqrt3}$, so $R=2r$.
A chord equal to the radius makes a triangle with two radii that has all sides equal, so the angle at the centre is $60^\circ$.
visual_proof: The altitude splits the triangle into two 30-60-90 halves with sides a/2, h, a; the centre sits on the altitude one-third of the way up.
shortcut: $h:R:r=3:2:1$; chord of central angle $\theta$ in a circle of radius $R$ is $2R\sin\frac\theta2$.
common_traps: Adding chords: PR = 14 is wrong because P, Q, R are not collinear.
Mixing up R and r: R = a/√3 is twice r = a/(2√3).
Not rationalising: 7√3 appears as 21/√3 in the options.

diagram.alt_text: Circle with centre O and radius 7. Chords PQ and QR each equal 7, so angles POQ and QOR are 60° each, and chord PR subtends 120°.

for P, Q in [(A, B), (B, C), (C, A)]:
    assert sp.simplify((P - Q).norm() - a) == 0

name: Pythagoras theorem
statement: c^2=a^2+b^2;\ 45\text{-}45\text{-}90 \text{ sides } 1:1:\sqrt2
derivation: Four copies of the right triangle placed in a square of side $a+b$ leave a tilted square of side $c$ in the middle.
Big square: $(a+b)^2=4\cdot\frac{ab}{2}+c^2$.
$a^2+2ab+b^2=2ab+c^2 \Rightarrow c^2=a^2+b^2$.
Isosceles right triangle: $c^2=a^2+a^2$, so $c=a\sqrt2$.
Converse: if $a^2+b^2=c^2$ the angle opposite $c$ is $90^\circ$.
visual_proof: Four copies of the triangle inside a square of side a + b leave a central square of area c²; rearranged they leave squares a² and b² instead.
common_traps: Stopping at QT = 8 (option A) and forgetting QR = 2 × QT.
Adding squares when the hypotenuse is known: √(17² + 15²) is not a leg.
In the converse test, the largest number must be c: check 5² + 12² = 13², not 5² + 13².

diagram.alt_text: Isosceles triangle PQR with PQ = PR = 17, altitude PT = 15 meeting QR at right angles, QT = TR = 8.

name: Triangle inequality
statement: |b-c|<a<b+c
conditions: \text{equality } a=b+c \text{ or } a=|b-c| \text{ means the points are collinear: no triangle}
derivation: The straight segment is the shortest path between two points, so $a<b+c$.
Apply the same to side $b$: $b<a+c$, so $a>b-c$; with side $c$: $a>c-b$.
Together: $|b-c|<a<b+c$.
At $a=b+c$ the third vertex lies on the segment: the triangle flattens into a line.
visual_proof: Hinge sides b and c at a vertex: closing the hinge shrinks the third side towards |b - c|, opening it flat stretches it towards b + c, and neither end is a real triangle.
shortcut: Integer third side with sides $p<q$: values $q-p+1,\dots,p+q-1$, count $=2p-1$. Each side $<$ half the perimeter.
common_traps: Using ≤ instead of <: counting 6 and 18 gives 13.
Counting 17 - 7 = 10 (option C) instead of 17 - 7 + 1 = 11.
Testing a smaller side against the other two proves nothing: test the largest side against the sum of the other two.

diagram.alt_text: Triangle with sides 6 and 12 hinged at a vertex and third side x; labels show 6 < x < 18.

import random
from fractions import Fraction as F
random.seed(0)

def exists(a, b, c):
    # a triangle with these sides exists iff the cosine rule gives -1 < cos A < 1
    cosA = (b * b + c * c - a * a) / (2 * b * c)
    return -1 < cosA < 1

n = 0
for _ in range(3000):
    a, b, c = (F(random.randint(1, 400), random.randint(1, 20)) for _ in range(3))
    assert exists(a, b, c) == (abs(b - c) < a < b + c)
    assert (abs(b - c) < a < b + c) == (a < b + c and b < c + a and c < a + b)
    n += 1

# boundaries: a = b + c and a = |b - c| are degenerate (collinear points, no triangle)
for _ in range(200):
    b, c = F(random.randint(1, 100)), F(random.randint(1, 100))
    assert not exists(b + c, b, c)                 # cos A = -1: A is a straight angle
    if b != c:
        assert not exists(abs(b - c), b, c)        # cos A = +1
    assert exists(b + c - F(1, 1000), b, c)
# worked example: sides 6, 12, x -> 6 < x < 18
xs = [x for x in range(1, 40) if exists(F(x), F(6), F(12))]
assert xs == list(range(7, 18)) and len(xs) == 11   # option A
# 11 + 13 = 24: X, Y, Z collinear
assert not exists(F(24), F(11), F(13))
print(f"CASES={n}")
print("BOUNDARY_OK")

name: Altitude on the hypotenuse
statement: h=\frac{ab}{c};\ h^2=pq \text{ (segments of the hypotenuse)}
derivation: Area two ways: $\frac12ab=\frac12ch$, so $h=\frac{ab}{c}$.
The altitude splits the triangle into two triangles similar to it and to each other (AA).
In the two small triangles: $\frac{h}{p}=\frac{q}{h}$, so $h^2=pq$.
Same similarity gives each leg: $b^2=pc$, $a^2=qc$.
visual_proof: The altitude from the right angle cuts the triangle into two smaller copies of itself; matching their sides gives h² = pq.
shortcut: Altitude $=$ geometric mean of the two hypotenuse pieces: $h=\sqrt{pq}$.
common_traps: Using the whole hypotenuse AB in place of AM: √(18 × 6) = 6√3, not CM.
Using the arithmetic mean (12 + 6)/2 = 9 instead of √(12 × 6).
Mixing up the leg rule: BC² = BM × AB, not BM × AM.

diagram.alt_text: Right triangle ABC with the right angle at C, hypotenuse AB = 18, and altitude CM to AB with AM = 12, BM = 6 and CM = 6√2.

name: Angle bisector theorem
statement: \frac{BD}{DC}=\frac{AB}{AC}
derivation: $AD$ bisects $\angle A$ and meets $BC$ at $D$.
$\triangle ABD$ and $\triangle ACD$ share the height from $A$, so $\frac{[ABD]}{[ACD]}=\frac{BD}{DC}$.
With $\frac12\cdot\text{side}\cdot AD\sin\frac A2$: $\frac{[ABD]}{[ACD]}=\frac{AB}{AC}$.
Equate: $\frac{BD}{DC}=\frac{AB}{AC}$.
visual_proof: The bisector foot D is equally far from AB and AC, so the two parts of the triangle have areas in the ratio AB : AC, and with a common apex these areas are also in the ratio BD : DC.
shortcut: $BD=\frac{AB}{AB+AC}\cdot BC$, $DC=\frac{AC}{AB+AC}\cdot BC$.
common_traps: Swapping the sides: NF goes with DF (the adjacent side), not DE; the swap gives 18 (option A).
Assuming the bisector hits the midpoint: 19 is not true unless DE = DF.
Using the ratio of the angles instead of the sides.

diagram.alt_text: Triangle DEF with DE = 36, DF = 40, EF = 38; the bisector of angle D meets EF at N, with EN = 18 and NF = 20.

name: Angle at the incentre
statement: \angle BIC=90^\circ+\frac{\angle A}2
derivation: $I$ is where the bisectors of $\angle B$ and $\angle C$ meet.
In $\triangle BIC$: $\angle BIC=180^\circ-\frac B2-\frac C2$.
$\frac{B+C}{2}=\frac{180^\circ-A}{2}=90^\circ-\frac A2$.
$\angle BIC=180^\circ-90^\circ+\frac A2=90^\circ+\frac A2$.
visual_proof: Triangle BIC keeps only half of angles B and C; the missing halves add to 90° - A/2, which the angle at I picks up.
shortcut: Incentre $90^\circ+\frac A2$; excentre $90^\circ-\frac A2$; orthocentre $180^\circ-A$; circumcentre $2A$.
common_traps: Stopping at P/2 = 17° (option D).
Using 180° - 107° = 73° as if O were the orthocentre.
Using the external-bisector formula 90° - A/2 and getting a negative angle.

diagram.alt_text: Triangle PQR with angle P = 34°. The bisectors of angles Q and R meet at the incentre O, and angle QOR = 107°.

import math, random
random.seed(0)

def angle(at, p, q):
    v1 = (p[0] - at[0], p[1] - at[1]); v2 = (q[0] - at[0], q[1] - at[1])
    cs = (v1[0] * v2[0] + v1[1] * v2[1]) / (math.hypot(*v1) * math.hypot(*v2))
    return math.degrees(math.acos(max(-1.0, min(1.0, cs))))

for _ in range(2000):
    A, B, C = [(random.uniform(-10, 10), random.uniform(-10, 10)) for _ in range(3)]
    if abs((B[0]-A[0])*(C[1]-A[1]) - (C[0]-A[0])*(B[1]-A[1])) < 1e-2:
        continue
    a, b, c = math.dist(B, C), math.dist(C, A), math.dist(A, B)
    I = tuple((a * A[i] + b * B[i] + c * C[i]) / (a + b + c) for i in range(2))

    assert math.isclose(angle(B, A, I), angle(B, I, C), abs_tol=1e-6)
    assert math.isclose(angle(C, A, I), angle(C, I, B), abs_tol=1e-6)
    assert math.isclose(angle(I, B, C), 90 + angle(A, B, C) / 2, abs_tol=1e-6)

assert P == 34                                    # option C

name: Medians and Apollonius theorem
statement: AB^2+AC^2=2(AD^2+BD^2);\ \text{centroid divides each median } 2:1
derivation: $D$ is the midpoint of $BC$; put $D$ at the origin, $B=(-m,0)$, $C=(m,0)$, $A=(x,y)$.
Median length: $m_a^2=\frac{2b^2+2c^2-a^2}{4}$.
Centroid $G=\frac{A+B+C}{3}$ lies on $AD$ with $AG:GD=2:1$.
visual_proof: Mirror the triangle in D to get a parallelogram ABA'C: its diagonals are 2AD and BC, and the sum of the squares of a parallelogram's diagonals equals the sum of the squares of its four sides.
shortcut: Equal medians $\Leftrightarrow$ equal opposite sides; three equal medians $\Rightarrow$ equilateral.
common_traps: Using BC² instead of BD² = (BC/2)² inside the bracket.
Dropping the factor 2 on the right side.
Reversing the centroid ratio: the longer part (2) is from the vertex, AG = 2/3 of AD.

diagram.alt_text: Triangle ABC with median AD to the midpoint D of BC and centroid G on AD, AG : GD = 2 : 1.

statement: DE\parallel BC \Rightarrow \frac{AD}{DB}=\frac{AE}{EC};\ \text{midpoint join}\parallel\text{third side}=\tfrac12\text{ of it}

name: Congruence criteria and CPCT
statement: SSS,\ SAS,\ ASA,\ AAS,\ RHS \Rightarrow \text{corresponding parts are equal (CPCT)};\ SSA, AAA \text{ are not criteria}
derivation: SSS: the cosine rule turns three sides into three fixed angles, so the shape is fixed.
SAS: two sides and the included angle fix the third side (cosine rule).
ASA / AAS: two angles fix the third ($180^\circ$ sum); one side then fixes the rest (sine rule).
RHS: hypotenuse and a leg fix the other leg (Pythagoras).
SSA fails: the side opposite the angle can swing to two positions; AAA fails: scaling keeps the angles.
visual_proof: For SSA, a circle of radius BC round B cuts the other arm of angle A at two points, giving two different triangles with the same two sides and angle.
shortcut: Congruent $\Rightarrow$ equal area and perimeter; the converse is false.

steps: Two sides equal and same perimeter: third side $=$ perimeter $-$ the two sides, also equal.
Three sides equal: congruent by SSS (B).
A, C, D fail: one side and angle, or the same base and height (so the same area), allow different shapes.

common_traps: Treating SSA (two sides and a non-included angle) as SAS.
Treating AAA as a criterion: it gives similar, not congruent, triangles.
Equal area does not mean congruent: same base and height fit infinitely many triangles.

    A, B, C = T[2], T[0], T[1]

name: Circle basics
statement: \text{one circle through 3 non-collinear points; diameter is the longest chord; equal chords} \iff \text{equal arcs}
conditions: the three points are not collinear (collinear points lie on no circle)
derivation: A point equidistant from $A$ and $B$ lies on the perpendicular bisector of $AB$.
For non-collinear $A, B, C$ the perpendicular bisectors of $AB$ and $BC$ are not parallel, so they meet in exactly one point $O$: the only centre, radius $OA$.
A chord at distance $d$ from the centre has length $2\sqrt{r^2-d^2}$ ([[f:geometry.chord-perpendicular-from-centre]]), largest at $d=0$: the diameter $2r$.
A chord with central angle $\theta$ has length $2r\sin\frac{\theta}{2}$, which rises steadily for $0^\circ<\theta\le180^\circ$: equal arcs $\iff$ equal central angles $\iff$ equal chords.
A chord extended both ways is a secant (meets the circle twice); a line meeting it once is a tangent.
visual_proof: Equal chords AB and CD joined to the centre give congruent isosceles triangles OAB and OCD (SSS), so their central angles, and hence their arcs, are equal.
shortcut: Longest chord = diameter $2r$, at distance $0$ from the centre; congruent arcs $\Rightarrow$ chords in ratio $1:1$.

steps: Congruent arcs $PAQ$ and $RBS$ subtend equal central angles $\theta$.

common_traps: Treating the arc ratio and chord ratio as different for congruent arcs: equal arcs always give $1:1$.
Giving the radius as the distance of the longest chord from the centre: the diameter passes through the centre, so the distance is $0$.
Calling an extended chord a tangent or a diameter: it meets the circle twice, so it is a secant.
Drawing a circle through three collinear points: none exists.

import random
from fractions import Fraction as F
random.seed(0)

def circumcentre(A, B, C):
    # O equidistant from A, B, C: two linear equations from the perpendicular bisectors
    a1, b1 = 2 * (B[0] - A[0]), 2 * (B[1] - A[1])
    c1 = B[0] ** 2 + B[1] ** 2 - A[0] ** 2 - A[1] ** 2
    a2, b2 = 2 * (C[0] - B[0]), 2 * (C[1] - B[1])
    c2 = C[0] ** 2 + C[1] ** 2 - B[0] ** 2 - B[1] ** 2
    det = a1 * b2 - a2 * b1
    if det == 0:
        return None
    return (F(c1 * b2 - c2 * b1, det), F(a1 * c2 - a2 * c1, det))

def d2(P, Q):
    return (P[0] - Q[0]) ** 2 + (P[1] - Q[1]) ** 2

def arc(X, Y, avoid):
    # angular measure (radians) of the arc X..Y not containing point `avoid`
    a, b, z = pos(X), pos(Y), pos(avoid)
    ccw = (b - a) % TAU
    return ccw if (z - a) % TAU > ccw else TAU - ccw

def angle(u, v):
    return math.acos(max(-1, min(1, u[0] * v[0] + u[1] * v[1])))

n = 0
while n < 1500:
    r = random.uniform(0.5, 5)
    P = (r * random.uniform(1.05, 6), 0.0)
    half = math.asin(r / P[0])                       # half-angle of the tangent cone
    t1, t2 = (math.pi + random.uniform(-half, half) * 0.999 for _ in range(2))
    if abs(t1 - t2) < 0.01:
        continue
    u1, u2 = (math.cos(t1), math.sin(t1)), (math.cos(t2), math.sin(t2))
    A, B = hits(P, u1, r); C, D = hits(P, u2, r)     # A, C near; B, D far
    lhs = angle(u1, u2)
    rhs = (arc(B, D, A) - arc(A, C, B)) / 2
    assert math.isclose(lhs, rhs, abs_tol=1e-7)
    # tangent and secant: T is the contact point on the upper tangent
    ut = (math.cos(math.pi - half), math.sin(math.pi - half))
    T = (P[0] + P[0] * math.cos(half) * ut[0], P[0] * math.cos(half) * ut[1])
    assert math.isclose(math.hypot(*T), r, rel_tol=1e-9)
    lhs_t = angle(ut, u1)
    rhs_t = (arc(T, B, A) - arc(T, A, B)) / 2
    assert math.isclose(lhs_t, rhs_t, abs_tol=1e-6)
    # two tangents: P = 180 - minor arc between contact points
    T2 = (T[0], -T[1])
    assert math.isclose(2 * half, math.pi - arc(T, T2, (-r, 0.0)), abs_tol=1e-9)
    n += 1
# worked example 2024-09-12_1600_Q01: near arc AC = 100, far arc BC = 160, arc AB = 100
assert 2 * 50 + 2 * 30 == 160 and 360 - 100 - 160 == 100
# boundary: P inside (two chords crossing) -> angle = half the SUM of the intercepted arcs
for _ in range(300):
    r = random.uniform(0.5, 5)
    P = (r * random.uniform(0, 0.95), r * random.uniform(-0.2, 0.2))
    if math.hypot(*P) >= r * 0.98:
        continue
    t1, t2 = random.uniform(0, math.pi), random.uniform(0, math.pi)
    if abs(t1 - t2) < 0.05:
        continue
    u1, u2 = (math.cos(t1), math.sin(t1)), (math.cos(t2), math.sin(t2))
    A, B = hits(P, u1, r); C, D = hits(P, u2, r)     # A, C on the negative side; B, D on the positive
    lhs = angle(u1, u2)                              # angle BPD
    assert math.isclose(lhs, (arc(B, D, A) + arc(A, C, B)) / 2, abs_tol=1e-7)
    # the outside rule fails here (difference, not sum)
    assert not math.isclose(lhs, (arc(B, D, A) - arc(A, C, B)) / 2, abs_tol=1e-3) or arc(A, C, B) < 1e-3
print(f"CASES={n}")
print("BOUNDARY_OK")

name: Diagonals of special quadrilaterals
statement: \text{parallelogram: bisect each other; rhombus/kite: perpendicular; rhombus } d_1^2+d_2^2=4a^2
derivation: Parallelogram $ABCD$, diagonals meeting at $M$: $\triangle AMB \cong \triangle CMD$ (ASA: $AB = CD$, alternate angles equal), so $AM = MC$ and $BM = MD$.
Rhombus or kite with $AB = AD$, $CB = CD$: $A$ and $C$ are each equidistant from $B$ and $D$, so both lie on the perpendicular bisector of $BD$: $AC \perp BD$.
Rhombus: the diagonals halve each other at right angles, so each side is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with legs $\frac{d_1}{2}$ and $\frac{d_2}{2}$.
Kite: the diagonal joining the vertices where equal sides meet splits it into two congruent triangles (SSS, [[f:geometry.congruence-criteria]]), so it bisects those two angles.
visual_proof: The rhombus's diagonals cut it into four congruent right triangles, each with legs d1/2 and d2/2 and hypotenuse a.
shortcut: Rhombus side $a = \frac12\sqrt{d_1^2 + d_2^2}$; a point equidistant from two opposite vertices of a rhombus lies on the other diagonal.

steps: $OP = OR$ puts $O$ on the perpendicular bisector of diagonal $PR$.
In a rhombus that bisector is diagonal $QS$, so $O$ lies on $QS$ inside the rhombus.
$S$, $O$, $Q$ are collinear with $O$ between them: $\angle SOQ = 180^\circ$ (C).

common_traps: Assuming any parallelogram has perpendicular or equal diagonals: perpendicular only for a rhombus, equal only for a rectangle.
Forgetting the halves: $d_1^2 + d_2^2 = a^2$ makes the side twice too long.

In a kite, using the wrong diagonal as the mirror line: only the one joining the vertices where equal sides meet ($BD$ in $AB = BC$, $AD = DC$) gives $\angle ABD = \angle CBD$ and $\angle ADB = \angle CDB$.

diagram.alt_text: Rhombus PQRS with diagonals PR = 8 and QS = 6 crossing at right angles at M; each side is 5. A point O on QS is equidistant from P and R.

import sympy as sp

x1, y1, x2, y2, a, t = sp.symbols('x1 y1 x2 y2 a t', real=True)
u, v = sp.Matrix([x1, y1]), sp.Matrix([x2, y2])
A, B, D = sp.Matrix([0, 0]), u, v
C = u + v                                                     # parallelogram ABCD
assert sp.simplify((A + C) / 2 - (B + D) / 2) == sp.zeros(2, 1)   # diagonals bisect each other
# rhombus: |u| = |v| = a
u, v = sp.Matrix([a, 0]), sp.Matrix([a * sp.cos(t), a * sp.sin(t)])
d1, d2 = u + v, v - u
assert sp.simplify(d1.dot(d2)) == 0                           # perpendicular diagonals
assert sp.simplify(d1.dot(d1) + d2.dot(d2) - 4 * a**2) == 0   # d1^2 + d2^2 = 4a^2
# kite (or rhombus): AB = AD and CB = CD force AC perpendicular to BD, for any coordinates
P = [sp.Matrix(sp.symbols(f'{n}x {n}y', real=True)) for n in 'ABCD']
A, B, C, D = P
sq = lambda X: X.dot(X)
identity = 2 * (A - C).dot(D - B) - ((sq(A - B) - sq(A - D)) - (sq(C - B) - sq(C - D)))
assert sp.expand(identity) == 0
# worked examples
assert 180 - 54 - 50 == 76                                    # 2024-09-19_1600_Q23
x, y = (68 - 2) // 3, (33 + 7) // 2
assert 3 * x + 2 == 68 and 2 * y - 7 == 33 and 2 * x + 3 * y == 104   # 2024-09-25_1230_Q04
# 2024-09-17_1230_Q13: rhombus P(-4,0) Q(0,3) R(4,0) S(0,-3); O with OP = OR lies on x = 0 (diagonal QS)
O = sp.Matrix([0, sp.Rational(6, 5)])
Pp, Q, R, S = sp.Matrix([-4, 0]), sp.Matrix([0, 3]), sp.Matrix([4, 0]), sp.Matrix([0, -3])
assert sq(O - Pp) == sq(O - R)
assert sp.acos((S - O).dot(Q - O) / sp.sqrt(sq(S - O) * sq(Q - O))) == sp.pi   # angle SOQ = 180
